Slides (black), the lecture notes (green — study guide written from the lecture by Mohammed Alessa, Mohammed Alsalamah & Abdulrahman Alomar) and every gift (red). Points the note writers marked "beyond notes" are shown as added boxes. Aldughaither has no paediatric chapter (appendicitis is in his Appendix chapter — see the Appendix lecture). Testicular torsion and foreign bodies aren't on the slides but are asked — they are at the end.

King Saud University logo (title slide) (1)
  • Common Pediatric & Neonatal Surgical Emergencies. Neonatal: malrotation/midgut volvulus · pyloric stenosis · Hirschsprung's disease · esophageal atresia ± fistula · anorectal malformation (imperforate anus). Pediatric: intussusception · acute appendicitis.
GroupConditionsRemember
Neonate (first 28 days)Malrotation / midgut volvulus · hypertrophic pyloric stenosis · Hirschsprung disease · esophageal atresia · anorectal malformationsCan also present later in childhood
Older childrenIntussusception · acute appendicitisAppendicitis = most common pediatric surgical emergency
  • Emergencies by age: EA ± TEF and ARM — at birth · Hirschsprung — no meconium by 24 h (can present at any age; short-segment → "chronic constipation", lecture case 12 y) · malrotation — ≈75% in month 1, +≈15% by 1 year · pyloric stenosis 4–8 weeks · intussusception 3 months–3 years · appendicitis peak 10–12 y, possible at any age.

1. Acute appendicitis

  • Most common cause of acute surgical abdomen in children and adolescents. Peak incidence 10–12 years. Increased rate of perforation in children.
  • Higher perforation rate because young / nonverbal children can't communicate pain → delayed diagnosis and presentation.

Anatomy & pathology

  • 6–9 cm long, worm-shaped, blind-ending tube. Arises from the posteromedial aspect of the caecum. The base is found at the convergence of the three taeniae coli.
  • Causes — unclear. Path: obstruction of the lumen (fecalith, lymphoid hyperplasia, foreign body, tumor, parasite).
  • Luminal obstruction → inflammation → perforation (if untreated).

History & examination

  • History: diffuse/periumbilical pain that eventually localizes to the RLQ · pain followed by nausea/vomiting · anorexia · fever · peritonitis pain worse with movement, walking (jumping test).
  • P/E: child looks unwell, lying still · tachycardia may be present · fever · dehydrated · tenderness/rebound in the RLQ · Rovsing's sign — RLQ tenderness when pressure is exerted in the LLQ · diffuse peritonitis may indicate perforation.
  • Pediatric pearl: ask the child to jump — refusal to jump because of pain is a useful sign of peritoneal irritation. Danger sign: diffuse peritonitis suggests perforation.
  • 10-year-old girl, fever, vomiting, RLQ pain for 2 days, RLQ rebound → acute appendicitis. 437 ×4

Differential diagnosis

  • Appendicitis · gastroenteritis · ovarian torsion · urinary tract infection · mesenteric lymphadenitis.
  • Ovarian torsion — particularly in females. Mesenteric lymphadenitis — the classic appendicitis mimic.

Investigations

  • Elevated WBC (mainly neutrophils) · urinalysis to exclude UTI.
  • Imaging: not always needed if the diagnosis is clear · > 6 mm, dilated, thick, hyperaemic appendix with adjacent inflammation.
  • US: good first line · no radiation hazards · may miss the appendix. CT scan: very accurate · radiation hazard.

CT and ultrasound of acute appendicitis

TestWhat it showsStrengths / limits
CBCLeukocytosisSupportive only
UrinalysisExcludes UTIRules out a mimic
Ultrasound — first-lineDiameter > 7 mm · hyperaemia · inflamed surrounding fat · periappendiceal fluidFast, no radiation; operator-dependent — the appendix may not be visualized
CT with IV contrastClearer visualizationOnly if ultrasound is inconclusive; radiation → minimize in children
  • Lecture pearl — image even when it looks classic: history and exam both point to appendicitis — do you run to theatre? No: order an ultrasound first (quick and easy) to exclude alternative diagnoses.
Slide: "imaging not always needed if the diagnosis is clear". Doctor in the lecture: order an ultrasound even when the picture is classic, and the 429 exam key agrees (US before appendectomy) — follow the doctor. If US isn't among the options, a clinically obvious appendicitis goes for appendectomy. Size cut-off: the slide (and standard criteria) say > 6 mm; the notes wrote > 7 mm — use 6 mm.
  • 10-year-old, RLQ pain, fever, vomiting, guarding, 38.5 °C, high WBC, clear urine → next step confirm with abdominal US. 429 ×2
  • 10-year-old, RLQ pain, fever, tenderness and guarding, high WBC (no US option) → urgent appendectomy. 427 ×2

Treatment

  • NPO · IV fluid · start antibiotics · urgent appendectomy (open vs laparoscopic). Patient can go home next day · no antibiotics required > 24 h post-operatively · fast recovery.
  • Gold standard: laparoscopic appendectomy. Early appendectomy prevents perforation. Pre-op bundle: NPO · IV fluids · broad-spectrum antibiotics · optimization.
  • Antibiotics only? Considered when operative/anaesthetic risk exceeds the risk of appendicitis — e.g. severe cardiac or respiratory disease.

Ruptured / perforated appendicitis

  • Usually results from delayed presentation/diagnosis/Rx · patient can become very sick (septic shock) · need urgent appendectomy unless an abscess cavity has developed.
  • Abscess → antibiotics + percutaneous drain + interval appendectomy in 6–8 weeks. Prolonged recovery · antibiotics post-operatively · high risk of superficial/deep abdominal infections (20%).
UncomplicatedPerforated
ApproachOptimize → laparoscopic appendectomySurgery generally still possible unless presentation is markedly delayed
Presents ≥ 5 days—Often nonoperative first: IV antibiotics ± US-guided percutaneous abscess drainage
RecoveryUsually discharged the next dayProlonged — often ≥ 1 week in hospital, then oral antibiotics
Recurrent infection—Risk ≈ 20%
Added explanationThe commonest long-term complication after any laparotomy/appendectomy — especially for perforation — is adhesive small-bowel obstruction. Infertility after perforated appendicitis in girls is debated and much less common.
  • 12-year-old girl after appendectomy for perforated appendicitis — commonest long-term complication → adhesive bowel obstruction. 432 ×2 426

2. Malrotation / midgut volvulus

  • Intestinal rotation: normal rotation transforms a simple, straight alimentary tube into the mature fixed and folded configuration present at birth.
  • Normal midgut rotation: 4–12 weeks of fetal life — 270° counterclockwise movement of the midgut.
  • Bilious vomiting in any child is a surgical emergency — malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise. (Lecturer focus.)
  • Normally the ascending and descending colon are fixed retroperitoneally; transverse and sigmoid remain mobile.
FeatureNormalMalrotation
RotationComplete 270° counterclockwiseAnything other than 270° → abnormal rotation / fixation
Small bowelDuodenum crosses the midline; DJ junction left of the spinePredominantly right-sided
ColonCaecum in the RLQ; ascending/descending colon fixedPredominantly left-sided
Mesenteric baseBroadNarrow → predisposes to volvulus
Peritoneal bands—Ladd bands → duodenal obstruction → bilious (green) vomiting
Added explanationIn malrotation the caecum fails to reach the RLQ and usually lies high — in the right upper quadrant / epigastrium — with Ladd's bands running from it across the duodenum to the right abdominal wall.
  • Infant with bowel obstruction, X-ray: enlarged gastric gas bubble, no distal bowel gas — where is the caecum? → RUQ. 439

What is the problem with malrotation?

  • Ladd's band obstructing the duodenum → bilious vomiting.
  • Midgut volvulus (twisting) → ischaemia and bowel gangrene.
  • If not identified quickly → death from septic shock. If the patient does not die → entire bowel loss (short bowel syndrome) — not compatible with life.
  • Narrow mesenteric base → midgut volvulus (twist around the mesenteric vessels) → vascular compromise → ischaemia → gangrene. Untreated: septic shock, multiorgan failure, death; extensive bowel loss → short bowel syndrome → possible intestinal transplantation.

Presentation

  • 75% present in the first month of life · 15% in the first year.
  • Cardinal symptom: BILIOUS VOMITING. Others: abdominal pain · abdominal wall erythema · distended abdomen (late) · rectal blood (not always).
  • P/E: lethargic · dehydrated · tachycardia, hypotension ± fever · distended upper abdomen (stomach) · distended abdomen (late) · peritonitis (late) · abdominal wall erythema (late).
  • Never forget: bilious (green) vomiting = a surgical emergency in any child. Keep this in mind for the rest of your career.
  • Neonate with bilious vomiting in the first 24 hours, no meconium yet, distension → malrotation with midgut volvulus (the emergency to exclude first). 441

Investigation

  • Abdominal X-ray: can be totally normal · dilated stomach.
  • Abdominal ultrasound: reversal of SMA/SMV orientation.
  • Upper GI contrast study: the most sensitive test to diagnose malrotation (gold standard). Takes time — should not be done if the patient has a picture of bowel ischaemia.

Normal duodenal C-loop vs malrotation on upper GI contrast (duodenum fails to cross the midline)

Malrotation — plain film, upper GI contrast with right-sided jejunum, and a dilated stomach

  • Don't trust the plain film: a normal abdominal X-ray never rules out malrotation/volvulus — if the child has bilious vomiting, keep going.
  • Upper GI study: normal — duodenal C-loop crosses the midline, DJ junction left of the spine, level with the pylorus. Abnormal — fails to cross the midline (contrast stays on the right); DJ anywhere else; corkscrew = volvulus. Water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin) preferred over barium when perforation is possible. CT generally avoided in neonates.
Added explanationOn ultrasound the SMV normally lies to the right of the SMA; reversal, or a "whirlpool" twist of the mesenteric vessels, suggests malrotation/volvulus.
  • 1-month-old, bilious vomiting, irritable, haemodynamically unstable, X-ray = high obstruction → next imaging → contrast upper GI study (if he is unstable with ischaemia, go straight to laparotomy). 442 ×2

Treatment

  • IV fluid · NPO · NGT · broad-spectrum antibiotics · immediate surgical consultation.
  • Urgent Ladd's procedure: laparotomy · untwist the bowel · resect gangrenous intestines · divide Ladd's band · place the bowel in non-rotation position (small intestine on the right, large intestine on the left) · appendectomy.
#StepWhy
1Detorse the bowelRestore perfusion
2Resect nonviable bowel, if presentRemove gangrenous bowel
3Divide Ladd bandsRelieve the duodenal obstruction
4Widen the mesenteric baseReduce the risk of recurrent volvulus
5Small bowel on the right, large bowel on the leftNonrotation position
6AppendectomyPrevents future diagnostic confusion from the abnormal appendix position
  • Why the appendectomy? The appendix ends up on the left, so a future appendicitis would not give classic RLQ pain — done to avoid diagnostic confusion, not to prevent recurrent volvulus.
  • 3-month-old with malrotation → open surgery (Ladd's procedure by laparotomy). 439

Delayed diagnosis / management

  • Bowel gangrene · short bowel syndrome · septic shock · multi-organ failure · death.

3. Intussusception

  • Part of the intestine telescopes into the distal bowel by peristaltic activity.
  • Bowel is compressed → venous obstruction → bowel wall oedema → arterial insufficiency → ischaemia & necrosis.
  • Causes: idiopathic — 95% (Peyer's patch). Pathologic lead point — 4%: Meckel diverticulum · polyp · neoplasm · inverted appendix · celiac disease, CF, HSP · feeding tubes (GJ tube).

Telescoping — like a collapsing telescope

Ileocolic intussusception — ileum telescoping through the ileocaecal valve into the colon

  • In children it is most commonly ileocolic / ileocaecal — the ileum telescopes into the caecum — though it can occur anywhere. Idiopathic cases: hypertrophied Peyer patches, often after a viral/upper respiratory infection ~2 weeks earlier. Clue to a lead point: recurrent episodes.
  • 18-month-old, URTI a week ago, colicky crying with legs drawn up, mass, blood and mucus PR — most common site → ileocolic. 438

Presentation

  • Typical age: 3 months–3 yrs. Episodic colicky abdominal pain · child is well between the attacks · bilious vomiting · red currant jelly stool · sausage-shaped abdominal mass in RUQ (65%) · empty RLQ.

Red currant jelly stool (dark blood mixed with mucus), redcurrants, and the sausage-shaped mass in the upper abdomen

  • Pain: intermittent, severe, colicky — crying, drawing knees to abdomen; symptom-free and comfortable between attacks, sometimes sleeping. Vomiting bilious (obstruction). Red currant jelly stool = the classic finding.
  • 2-year-old, 6 h of episodic crying, unwell, tachycardic, blood with mucus PR, US target sign → intussusception. 442 ×7

Investigations

  • US: gold standard — target sign. AXR: RUQ mass, dilated bowel, air/fluid levels.
  • 18-month-old, 6 h of episodic crying, legs pulled up, upper abdominal mass → best imaging abdominal ultrasound. 438 ×5

Management

  • NPO · IVF · reduction enema under fluoroscopic guidance (done by a radiologist). Surgical reduction if enema reduction is not successful or not available.

Contrast enema reduction and laparoscopic reduction

  • Resuscitate (NPO · IV fluids · antibiotics) → therapeutic enema, first line → surgical reduction if it fails/unavailable → resection ± temporary stoma if nonreducible/necrotic.
  • Enema technique: air, contrast or saline; rectal catheter with an adequate seal; gradual, controlled pressure; careful to avoid perforation. Success = reflux of contrast/air into the small bowel.
Added explanationSkip the enema — go to surgery when there is peritonitis, perforation (free air) or shock / haemodynamic instability.
  • 1-year-old, intermittent pain with hip flexion, distension, red currant jelly stool, RUQ mass, target sign → initial management contrast enema. 439 ×5

Recurrence

  • Can recur, particularly in the first 24–48 hours; lecture estimate ≈ 20%. Recurrent episodes suggest a pathological lead point; > 3 episodes → operative exploration.
Doctor: recurrence ≈ 20%. Book: about 10% after enema reduction (lower after surgery). Use the doctor's figure for his questions.

4. Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis

  • Gastric outlet obstruction due to hypertrophied pyloric muscle.
  • Classic triad: term baby · 2–8 weeks of life · projectile, non-bilious vomiting.
  • Hungry & dehydrated baby · palpable pyloric muscle (olive sign) · gastric peristalsis can sometimes be seen.
  • Electrolytes + blood gas: hypochloraemia · hypokalaemia · metabolic alkalosis.
  • Who/when: predominantly full-term infants, males > females, typically 4–8 weeks. "A hungry baby who can feed but cannot empty the stomach." Non-bilious because the obstruction is proximal to bile entry.
  • Very important — hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis: Cl⁻ and H⁺ lost as HCl in vomitus; K⁺ lost by the kidney (volume depletion → aldosterone).
  • 6-week-old, projectile non-bilious vomiting labelled GERD, no response to ranitidine, now dehydrated, X-ray unremarkable → pyloric stenosis. 434 ×2

Imaging & management

  • US: gold standard — thick and elongated pyloric muscle.
  • Management: NPO · IVF · correct electrolytes and pH · surgical separation of pyloric muscles (pyloromyotomy).

Pyloromyotomy — the hypertrophied muscle split down to the mucosa

  • Resuscitate always before surgery — correct dehydration, electrolytes and the alkalosis; NG decompression if needed. Pyloric stenosis is not a reason to rush to theatre.
  • Pyloromyotomy (laparoscopic or open): longitudinal division of the muscle without entering the mucosa · no bowel resection · intra-operative saline/air leak test to exclude mucosal perforation.
  • 4-week-old, non-bilious projectile vomiting after every feed, hungry, mildly dehydrated → best initial imaging abdominal ultrasound. 442
  • Pyloric stenosis — best management → pyloromyotomy (after resuscitation). 439 ×4

5. Esophageal atresia ± tracheoesophageal fistula

  • Interruption in the continuity of the esophagus with or without fistula. Caused by error in separation of esophagus & trachea (4th week gestation). 1:4500 live births · male > female · 50–60% associated anomalies.
  • VACTERL: Vertebral, Anal, Cardiac, TracheoEsophageal, Renal, Limb.
  • Types: A isolated EA (gasless abdomen) · B EA + proximal TEF (rare, gasless) · C proximal blind pouch + distal TEF — ≈ 85%, most common · D proximal + distal TEF (rare) · E isolated H-type TEF (no atresia, aspiration).
  • VACTERL screening: V spine X-ray ± spinal US · A screen for ARM · C echocardiography · TE check oesophageal patency · R renal US · L skeletal survey. One VACTERL anomaly → screen for all the others.
Added explanationGas in the abdomen on X-ray means a distal fistula (types C, D, E); a gasless abdomen means no distal fistula (types A, B).

Presentation & management

  • Prenatal: polyhydramnios. Postnatal: drooling · vomiting · respiratory distress · resistance upon insertion of NGT (coiled in the chest).
  • The diagnosis is made primarily by failure of NG tube passage, with imaging showing the tube coiled in the upper pouch — the classic finding.
  • Management: urgent surgery · right thoracotomy · division of fistula · repair esophagus.

Positioning for right thoracotomy and repair — fistula divided, oesophageal ends anastomosed

Added explanationWhile awaiting surgery: continuous suction of the upper pouch (Replogle tube) and head-up positioning to limit aspiration.

6. Imperforate anus — anorectal malformation (ARM)

  • Various forms of anorectal anomaly. Normal anus: normal size, located at the centre of the muscle sphincter. 1:4000 · male > female · 65% have associated anomalies (VACTERL).
  • "ARM" is the preferred term. Normal anus ≈ midway between the coccyx and the scrotal base / vulva. Inspect every newborn perineum — then give the fistula ~24 hours to declare itself.
  • Females: perineal fistula · rectovestibular fistula · cloaca (single opening for urethra, vagina and rectum). Males: perineal fistula · rectourethral fistula · rectovesical fistula. Both: imperforate anus without fistula · rectal atresia.

Vestibular fistula — diagram and newborn girl (fistula in the posterior vestibule)

Perineal fistula — diagram and male infant with a meconium-filled subepithelial tract along the raphe

Assessment & surgical options

  • Inspect the perineum (anal opening? location? meconium?) → wait ≈ 24 h for fistula/meconium → prone cross-table lateral X-ray (invertogram): mark the expected anus on the skin and measure the distance to the distal rectal gas. Meconium: girls — vestibule/vagina; boys — perineal/scrotal skin or urine. Subcutaneous meconium can show as beading along a fistulous track.
  • Surgical options: primary anoplasty · colostomy with delayed anoplasty.

Prone cross-table lateral films — low pouch near the skin marker (primary anoplasty) vs high pouch far from it (colostomy first)

Added explanationVisible perineal fistula (either sex) → anoplasty in the newborn period, no colostomy. No fistula after 24 h: rectal gas < 1 cm from the marker → primary PSARP; > 1 cm → colostomy first, PSARP later. Rectourethral/rectovesical fistula or cloaca → colostomy, staged repair.

7. Hirschsprung's disease

  • Absence of ganglion cells in the myenteric & submucosal plexus. Arrest in ganglion-cell migration from proximal to distal GI tract. Transition zone: area between normal & aganglionic bowel.
  • Types: 80% rectosigmoid TZ · 10% proximal colon TZ · 5% total colonic HD · rare near-total intestinal HD.
  • No ganglion cells, no relaxation → functional intestinal obstruction. The dilated proximal bowel is normal — it expands only because stool cannot pass the non-relaxing distal segment.

Presentation

  • Neonatal: delayed passage of meconium > 24 h · bilious vomiting · abdominal distension · feeding intolerance. Delayed: chronic refractory constipation · abdominal distension · failure to thrive.
  • Short-segment disease is often mislabelled "chronic constipation" — failure to thrive, thin wasted limbs with a hugely distended abdomen (lecture case: 12-year-old, caecum ≈ 20 cm full of stool).
Added explanationHirschsprung-associated enterocolitis — fever, distension and explosive, foul-smelling diarrhoea; before or after surgery; can progress to sepsis. The explosive gush of gas and stool after rectal examination is a classic sign.
  • 3-week-old, 2 weeks of distension, needs anal stimulation to pass stool, explosive foul gas/feces on PR, no rectal air → Hirschsprung disease. 437 ×6
  • 3-year-old with constipation — the feature pointing to a surgical cause → delayed passage of meconium > 48 h after birth. 434 ×2

Diagnosis

  • Rectal manometry: absent recto-anal inhibitory reflex · contrast study · rectal biopsy — gold standard (look for ganglion cells in the myenteric & submucosal plexus).
  • Contrast enema supports the diagnosis (narrow distal bowel, transition zone, small rectum with dilated sigmoid) — not definitive. Rectal suction biopsy = gold standard — bedside, generally not painful; absent ganglion cells confirm.
  • One-day-old who hasn't passed meconium (Hirschsprung) — how to investigate → contrast (barium) enema, then rectal suction biopsy to confirm. 441

Treatment

  • Resection of aganglionic bowel · pull-through procedure.
  • Usually laparoscopic(-assisted); intra-op biopsies confirm the ganglionated level. Follow up into adulthood (≈ 18 years): constipation, anastomotic stricture, bowel-function problems.

  • Bilious vomiting = obstruction distal to bile entry → surgical emergency (malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise). Non-bilious projectile vomiting = proximal → pyloric stenosis; resuscitate and correct the alkalosis first.

9. Other emergencies asked (not on the slides)

Testicular torsion

Added explanationTesticular torsion — sudden severe scrotal pain with nausea/vomiting, a high-riding, horizontally lying, very tender testis and an absent cremasteric reflex. It is a clinical diagnosis: urgent scrotal exploration without waiting for imaging; detorse, and fix both testes (bell-clapper deformity is usually bilateral). Salvage is high within 6 hours and falls steeply after that — the testis is usually lost by 12–24 h.
  • Boy, sudden scrotal pain at 2 am, vomiting, absent cremasteric reflex, tender horizontal right testis → scrotal exploration. 429
  • Left testicular torsion — best management → bilateral (right and left) orchidopexy. 439
  • Ischaemia time until torsion injury becomes irreversible → 6–12 hours. 438

Foreign body aspiration & ingestion

Added explanationInhaled foreign body (peanut) — choking episode, then cough, wheeze or stridor, unilateral decreased air entry and hyperinflation of that lung (ball-valve). First secure the airway if there is distress or cyanosis; then rigid bronchoscopy to remove it.
  • 9-month-old, sudden cough, stridor and cyanosis while eating peanuts → first step try to secure his airway. 429 ×3 427
  • 2-year-old, choking episode, stridor, decreased right air entry, right lung hyperinflation, sats 98% → bronchoscopy. 437 ×9
Added explanationSwallowed foreign body already in the stomach in an asymptomatic child (a small blunt object) → usually passes: observe with serial X-rays. Urgent endoscopy for button batteries in the oesophagus, multiple magnets, sharp objects or symptoms.
  • 12-year-old, swallowed small metallic toy 6 h ago, asymptomatic, FB in the stomach → re-evaluate with X-rays. 434 ×2
